author: sleepinyourhat
text: We gave bonuses to our writers for each question of theirs that made it into this subset. This is basically adversarial data collection, but with humans instead of an ML model as the adversary. https://t.co/0Eukkx4B3V

author: sleepinyourhat
text: The difficult subset—about half of the total dataset—consists only of validated examples that these rushed annotators couldn’t solve, suggesting that they require relatively subtle or holistic reading comprehension.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: Accuracy in this setting is much worse, despite evidence that annotators were trying hard here, and running this validation let us create a difficult subset of the data.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: We also did a second round of validation on MTurk, where we let annotators spend only 45 seconds on each question. They could skim or search the text, but they didn’t have enough time to read it carefully.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: We validated the questions on MTurk, but paid well enough that our annotators were able to spend an hour on each article/story reading and answering questions. It seems like they took this seriously: Human annotator accuracy on our data is over 93%.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: We hired a small team of great writers on Upwork to write our questions. Most of them have humanities degrees, and many of them have professional experience writing or grading reading comprehension tests.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: But we did the (relatively) hard, slow, expensive thing instead, and I think it paid off pretty well:

author: sleepinyourhat
text: Collecting examples using passages this long is cumbersome, and it’s tempting to use shortcuts here, like adversarial data collection or writing questions based on *summaries* of the input texts.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: The questions are multiple-choice: We made a bet that it’d be possible to build a hard, subtle, unambiguous multiple-choice dataset, and sticking to this format this means that it’ll be easy to measure model performance.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: It’s a set of reading comprehension questions about articles and short stories of 2k–8k tokens (words + punctuation). That’s about a 30-minute read on average. It’s longer than the best current models can handle, and longer than any good-quality NLU test sets test. https://t.co/XjQVFCoQ49

author: sleepinyourhat
text: The paper sketches out a few things we can do to try to get better about this. Better benchmarks and better analysis tools should help a lot, if only by calming down the hype cycle a bit. But a lot of the issue is just careful writing.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: The argument in this paper is simple: The stakes are getting higher for what we do. We should be careful about the claims we make. Putting a sloppy or unjustified claim in a paper is a problem whether that claim is about what we can do or what we can't.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: Not really. It's important that we build a clear consensus on what kind of progress we are and aren't making in NLP. That means avoiding hype, but it also means acknowledging the progress that we do make.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: So, if overselling and hype are such a problem, it's probably best to just do the opposite, and avoid almost any positive-sounding claims about what systems can do. Right?

author: sleepinyourhat
text: Overstating results about your system is bad science. Overstating results about other peoples' systems means buying into hype, and that's just embarrassing. Overstating any results could lead more people to recklessly deploy technology brittle, biased technology.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: I think there's a good scientific instinct behind these claims:

author: sleepinyourhat
text: That kind of claim masks the huge difference between the small trained-from-scratch LSTMs of 2017 and newer models like GPT-3 or FLAN that barely use labeled training data at all. Newer systems are far less brittle, and they're not brittle in the same ways.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: Lots of *recent* NLP papers cite Jia and Liang as evidence for a claim like "neural networks are brittle and can't really do reading comprehension".

author: sleepinyourhat
text: The paper itself is excellent, and it has some really surprising results about how brittle early SQuAD models were. The issue is how the paper has been cited since then:

author: sleepinyourhat
text: I pick on the Jia and Liang (2017) adversarial SQuAD paper a bit here, for example. https://t.co/ASsNEzhOOG

author: sleepinyourhat
text: This often means saying that today's models don't work but only citing evidence for much older models. Or setting up adversarial evaluations that any system would fail, no matter how good it is. This paper goes through a bunch of examples of what this looks like.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: I see a lot of authors in NLP lately who seem to be going far out of their way to write that current systems don't really work well.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: After all that big flashy setup, the main argument of this paper is actually about something pretty small and pretty concrete:

author: sleepinyourhat
text: So, if you work on NLP, and you're concerned about whether your career winds up making the world a better place, then it really matters whether we see impacts like this coming early enough to prepare.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: Overpreparing is a waste. Underpreparing is a disaster.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: If this is even a little bit plausible, we should do something about it. Preparing for those impacts—figuring out how to get more of the good and less of the bad—is going to be hard work, and we'll need all the time we can get.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: I don't think that we're close to any of that. I don't know how we'd get there. But if you draw out our current rate of progress for fifteen or twenty-five or fifty years, this kind of really transformative impact really does seem possible.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: Plus, mass political surveillance is easy now. A few lucky tech companies are becoming *even more* powerful, to the point that they're basically unaccountable. Some of the science-fiction 'AI goes badly' scenarios stop looking so crazy.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: But that's not the whole story. Algorithmic bias and data governance? The stakes there just got a lot higher. And half the service sector is out of a job. Most translators are out of a career.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: We can build some incredibly valuable stuff. Great education, medical advice, and legal advice become universally accessible worldwide, in any language. Many kinds of important research get dramatically easier.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: So what happens if we figure out how to build systems that are broadly effective at language and reasoning?

author: sleepinyourhat

author: sleepinyourhat
text: @code_star Yeah, definitely. Good blog posts *for a technical audience* can be really valuable. See also @distillpub (RIP 😢).

author: sleepinyourhat
text: @shortstein In the unlikely hypothetical where you submit a paper *knowing in advance* that nobody will ever use your findings, I'd argue that's quite bad, even if the paper does get accepted.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: @shortstein That really does seem like a failure. It's not always foreseeable/avoidable, but it seems worth taking steps to try to avoid.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: @shortstein I don't think that _low_ engagement means something is pointless, but I'm mainly thinking of cases of _zero_ engagement, or at least zero engagement by people who actually care about the work.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: @code_star (I don't think I'm saying anything at all weird/specific, just that you should have some actual goal in mind when you write up your research.)

author: sleepinyourhat
text: @code_star ...but for more theoretical/technical work without such direct implications, the goal should mainly be to reach other technical people, wherever they are.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: @code_star For example, public-facing blog posts seem pretty good for work that directly addresses what kinds of applications we can/can't build trustworthy models for...

author: sleepinyourhat
text: @code_star Maybe! How you rewrite/present it will depend on which audience would actually be able to do something with what you've learned.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: In short, it's bad that so much of academic publishing is an empty status game. If you're participating in it in a way that doesn't advance our collective knowledge or abilities, something has gone wrong, and you should be worried.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: ...since the papers you're assigned will be, on average, both much less trustworthy and much less relevant to you than the papers you would have chosen on your own.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: I think it was my co-advisor @chrmanning who first pointed out to me that reviewing *so that you accomplish your goal of reading more papers* is bad strategy, ...

author: sleepinyourhat
text: In addition, I think this situation makes look reviewing look *less* valuable as service work, not more. You should still do your part, but it's reasonable to be a bit depressed about it.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: In many cases, though, outside stakeholders will want to see evidence that the ideas/artifacts that you're sharing with them got a scientific stamp of approval. In these cases, the 'stamp of approval' of a paper acceptance is much more clearly creating value.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: I acknowledge that this second strategy doesn't exactly mitigate the harms I'd mentioned, since the reviewers are still reviewing something that won't get read.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: (ii) figuring out how to have your research have a more direct impact on the world *even if it doesn't get read*, prehaps by releasing concrete artifacts, working with relevant non-academic stakeholders, or rewriting results for an interested public.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: (i) figuring out how to get your work read by the people who should read it, either through your choice of topic, your writing, or self-promotion (not a dirty word!), and...

author: sleepinyourhat
text: So the problem is to figure out how to prevent this from happening. This means some combination of...

author: sleepinyourhat
text: Even if you learned something from doing the research, all the time you spend writing it up, plus the time that the reviewers/editors/ACs spend on it, is a deadweight loss. While the paper might advance your career a bit (not much!), it doesn't create value for anyone else.

author: sleepinyourhat

text: @todd_gureckis Yeah—I think that's part of the issue. The IRB framework is set up to focus mainly on studies where there is potential to harm the research subjects. If you're trying to set up new/expanded reviewing norms for NLP research, that doesn't seem like the right emphasis.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: @todd_gureckis Also, there's lots of room for projects that would likely be harmful if deployed. Work on detecting coded political speech, or work on inferring criminality/mental illness from public posts?

author: sleepinyourhat
text: @todd_gureckis Scraping/organizing/releasing personal web data in a more public form than the original is a big one—not clear that that always counts as human subjects research if there's no intent to _study_ the data owners.

author: sleepinyourhat
text: Blgh. Do we have to follow the IRB model? It's pretty terribly suited to NLP-style work: Dramatically slows down work that *obviously* has no reasonable risk to subjects; doesn't even consider risk to non-subject third parties, which can be serious.

author: sleepinyourhat
